prompt: What structural unit do all the carbonyl compounds in Table 18.14.1 contain?

choices.text: An acyl group, R–C=O, bonded to another substituent
An –OH group bonded to the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: Only carboxylic acids have an –OH group on the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: An –OR group bonded to the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: Only esters and lactones have an –OR group there.

choices.text: A carbon–carbon double bond next to the carbonyl group
choices.why: The unit they all share is the acyl group, R–C=O.

explanation: All the compounds in Table 18.14.1 contain an acyl group (R–C=O) bonded to another substituent. R can be practically any organic part, and the other substituent might be a carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, halogen, nitrogen, or sulfur.

prompt: According to Table 18.14.1, which name ending is used for esters?

choices.text: -oate
-al
choices.why: -al is the ending for aldehydes.

choices.text: -one
choices.why: -one is the ending for ketones.

choices.text: -thioate
choices.why: -thioate is the ending for thioesters.

explanation: Esters take the ending -oate. For comparison, Table 18.14.1 gives -al for aldehydes, -one for ketones, -oic acid for carboxylic acids, -thioate for thioesters, and -amide for amides.

prompt: Table 18.14.1 lists "None" as the name ending for two kinds of carbonyl compounds. Which two?

choices.text: Lactones and lactams
Aldehydes and ketones
choices.why: Aldehydes end in -al and ketones in -one.

choices.text: Acid halides and acid anhydrides
choices.why: Acid halides end in -yl or -oyl halide, and anhydrides in -oic anhydride.

choices.text: Thioesters and amides
choices.why: Thioesters end in -thioate and amides in -amide.

explanation: Lactones (cyclic esters) and lactams (cyclic amides) have no characteristic name ending in Table 18.14.1.

prompt: Why are aldehydes and ketones placed in a different category from carboxylic acids and their derivatives?

choices.text: Their acyl group is bonded to H or C, which can't act as a leaving group
Their acyl group is bonded to O, N, S, or a halogen, which can act as a leaving group
choices.why: That describes carboxylic acids and their derivatives, not aldehydes and ketones.

choices.text: They have no carbonyl group
choices.why: Aldehydes and ketones do contain the C=O group; they appear in Table 18.14.1.

choices.text: Their carbonyl carbon is sp3-hybridized
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon is sp2-hybridized in all carbonyl compounds.

explanation: In an aldehyde or ketone, the acyl group is bonded to H or C, atoms that can't stabilize a negative charge and so can't act as leaving groups in a nucleophilic substitution. In carboxylic acids and their derivatives it is bonded to oxygen, halogen, sulfur, or nitrogen, which can stabilize a negative charge and act as leaving groups.

prompt: Which of these carbonyl compounds lacks a leaving group that could be replaced in a nucleophilic substitution?

choices.text: A ketone
An ester
choices.why: An ester's acyl group is bonded to oxygen, which can stabilize a negative charge and act as a leaving group.

choices.text: An amide
choices.why: An amide's acyl group is bonded to nitrogen, which the section lists among the atoms that can act as leaving groups.

choices.text: An acid halide
choices.why: An acid halide's halogen can stabilize a negative charge and act as a leaving group.

explanation: A ketone's acyl group is bonded to a carbon, which can't stabilize a negative charge, so ketones (like aldehydes) have no appropriate leaving group. Esters, amides, and acid halides have O, N, or a halogen on the acyl carbon, which can act as leaving groups.

prompt: How is the carbonyl carbon bonded?

choices.text: It is sp2-hybridized, with three σ bonds and a π bond to oxygen from p-orbital overlap
It is sp3-hybridized, with four σ bonds
choices.why: A tetrahedral sp3 carbon forms only after a nucleophile adds. The carbonyl carbon itself is sp2.

choices.text: It is sp-hybridized, with two σ bonds and two π bonds
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond.

choices.text: It is sp2-hybridized, with a π bond from overlap of two sp2 orbitals
choices.why: The π bond comes from sideways overlap of a carbon p orbital with an oxygen p orbital.

explanation: The carbonyl carbon atom is sp2-hybridized and forms three σ bonds. Its fourth valence electron remains in a carbon p orbital and forms a π bond to oxygen by overlapping with an oxygen p orbital, much like the C=C bond of an alkene.

prompt: How many nonbonding electron pairs does the oxygen atom of a carbonyl group have?
explanation: Besides its σ and π bonds to carbon, the carbonyl oxygen atom has two nonbonding pairs of electrons, which occupy its remaining two orbitals.

prompt: What is the approximate bond angle around a carbonyl carbon, in degrees?
explanation: Like alkenes, carbonyl compounds are planar about the double bond and have bond angles of approximately 120° (Figure 18.14.1 shows the structure of acetaldehyde).

prompt: How long is a carbon–oxygen double bond, in picometers?
explanation: The carbon–oxygen double bond is both shorter and stronger than a C–O single bond: 122 pm versus 143 pm, and 732 kJ/mol versus 385 kJ/mol.

prompt: A C=O double bond has a strength of 732 kJ/mol, and a C–O single bond has a strength of 385 kJ/mol. How much stronger is the double bond, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 732 kJ/mol − 385 kJ/mol = 347 kJ/mol. The carbon–oxygen double bond is both shorter (122 pm versus 143 pm) and stronger than a C–O single bond.

prompt: Which statement describes the polarity of the carbonyl group?

choices.text: The carbon is δ+ and electrophilic; the oxygen is δ− and nucleophilic
The carbon is δ− and nucleophilic; the oxygen is δ+ and electrophilic
choices.why: That's reversed. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so oxygen carries the partial negative charge.

choices.text: The carbon is δ+ but nucleophilic; the oxygen is δ− but electrophilic
choices.why: A δ+ carbon is an electrophilic (Lewis acidic) site, and a δ− oxygen is a nucleophilic (Lewis basic) site.

choices.text: The C=O bond is nonpolar, like the C=C bond of an alkene
choices.why: Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is strongly polarized.

explanation: The carbon–oxygen double bond is strongly polarized because of oxygen's high electronegativity. The carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge, is an electrophilic (Lewis acidic) site, and reacts with nucleophiles. The oxygen carries a partial negative charge, is a nucleophilic (Lewis basic) site, and reacts with electrophiles.

prompt: Most reactions of carbonyl compounds take place by one of four general mechanisms. Which of these is NOT one of the four?

choices.text: Electrophilic addition
Nucleophilic addition
choices.why: Nucleophilic addition is one of the four; it is the most common reaction of aldehydes and ketones (Chapter 19).

choices.text: Alpha substitution
choices.why: Alpha substitution is one of the four; it occurs at the position next to the carbonyl group (Chapter 22).

choices.text: Carbonyl condensation
choices.why: Carbonyl condensation is one of the four; it occurs when two carbonyl compounds react with each other (Chapter 23).

explanation: The four general mechanisms are nucleophilic addition, nucleophilic acyl substitution, alpha substitution, and carbonyl condensation. Electrophilic addition is the characteristic reaction of alkenes.

prompt: When a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone, what happens to that carbon?

choices.text: It rehybridizes from sp2 to sp3, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide
It rehybridizes from sp3 to sp2, giving a planar alkoxide
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon starts out sp2 and becomes sp3.

choices.text: It stays sp2, so the product remains planar
choices.why: The new bond to the nucleophile gives the carbon four groups, so it becomes tetrahedral and sp3.

choices.text: It rehybridizes from sp2 to sp, giving a linear product
choices.why: Gaining a fourth group makes the carbon tetrahedral, not linear.

explanation: The nucleophile uses an electron pair to form a new bond to carbon, and two electrons from the carbon–oxygen double bond move toward oxygen, giving an alkoxide anion. The carbonyl carbon rehybridizes from sp2 to sp3, so the alkoxide ion product has tetrahedral geometry.

prompt: After a nucleophile adds to an aldehyde or ketone, what can the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate do next?

choices.text: Be protonated to an alcohol, or be protonated and lose the oxygen to form C=Nu
Expel H− or R− as a leaving group to re-form a C=O bond
choices.why: H and C can't stabilize a negative charge, so they can't act as leaving groups.

choices.text: Lose an α hydrogen to become an enolate ion
choices.why: Enolate ions form when carbonyl compounds react with strong base. The tetrahedral alkoxide is protonated.

choices.text: Nothing further; the alkoxide anion is always the final product
choices.why: The alkoxide is protonated, either to an alcohol or on the way to a C=Nu double bond.

explanation: Depending on the nucleophile, the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is either protonated by water or acid to form an alcohol, or protonated and then expels the oxygen to form a new double bond between the carbonyl carbon and the nucleophile (Figure 18.14.2).

prompt: When an aldehyde or ketone is reduced with NaBH4 or LiAlH4, what nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon?

choices.text: A hydride ion, H:^−
A carbanion, R3C:^−
choices.why: A carbanion is the nucleophile in a Grignard reaction.

choices.text: A hydroxide ion, OH−
choices.why: Reduction adds hydride, which becomes a new C–H bond.

choices.text: A proton, H+
choices.why: H+ is an electrophile. It protonates the alkoxide after the addition step.

explanation: During a reduction with NaBH4 or LiAlH4, the nucleophile that adds to the carbonyl group is a hydride ion, H:^−. During a Grignard reaction it is a carbanion, R3C:^−. In both cases the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is then protonated to give an alcohol.

prompt: What forms when an aldehyde or ketone reacts with a primary amine, RNH2?

choices.text: An imine, R2C=NR′, after the intermediate loses water
An alcohol, after the tetrahedral alkoxide is protonated
choices.why: With amines, the alkoxide isn't isolated; it is protonated and loses water to form a C=N bond.

choices.text: An amide, by nucleophilic acyl substitution
choices.why: Aldehydes and ketones have no leaving group, so they don't undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution.

choices.text: An enolate ion, by loss of an α hydrogen
choices.why: The amine adds to the carbonyl carbon. Enolate ions form when carbonyl compounds react with strong base.

explanation: Aldehydes and ketones react with primary amines to form imines, R2C=NR′. The tetrahedral intermediate is the same kind formed in hydride reduction and Grignard reactions, but here it is protonated and then loses water to form the C=N double bond (Figure 18.14.3).

prompt: Why does nucleophilic acyl substitution occur with carboxylic acid derivatives but not with aldehydes and ketones?

choices.text: Acid derivatives have a leaving group on the carbonyl carbon that the intermediate can expel
Aldehydes and ketones don't react with nucleophiles at all
choices.why: They do react with nucleophiles; they undergo nucleophilic addition.

choices.text: Acid derivatives form planar intermediates instead of tetrahedral ones
choices.why: Both form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Only acid derivatives can then expel a leaving group.

choices.text: Acid derivatives have a carbonyl oxygen that acts as the leaving group
choices.why: The carbonyl oxygen stays. The leaving group is the atom or group bonded to the carbonyl carbon, such as –Cl or –OR.

explanation: Addition to a carboxylic acid derivative gives the usual tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, but because the derivative has a leaving group bonded to the carbonyl carbon, the intermediate expels it and forms a new carbonyl compound. The net effect is replacement of the leaving group by the entering nucleophile.

prompt: What happens in an alpha-substitution reaction of a carbonyl compound?

choices.text: An α hydrogen is replaced by an electrophile through an enol or enolate ion
The carbonyl oxygen is replaced by a nucleophile, forming C=Nu
choices.why: That is the C=Nu mode of nucleophilic addition, as in imine formation.

choices.text: The leaving group on the carbonyl carbon is replaced by a nucleophile
choices.why: That is nucleophilic acyl substitution.

choices.text: An α hydrogen is replaced by a nucleophile through a carbocation
choices.why: The α position reacts with an electrophile, through an enol or enolate ion intermediate.

explanation: Alpha substitution occurs at the position next to the carbonyl group, the α position. An α hydrogen is replaced by an electrophile through an intermediate enol or enolate ion. The carbonyl group makes the α hydrogens acidic, so carbonyl compounds react with strong base to give enolate ions.

prompt: How does an enolate ion react with a primary alkyl halide?

choices.text: As a nucleophile in an S_N2 reaction, forming a new C–C bond
As an electrophile that accepts the halide ion
choices.why: Enolate ions are negatively charged and act as nucleophiles.

choices.text: As a base in an E2 reaction that gives an alkene
choices.why: The section shows enolates reacting with primary alkyl halides by S_N2, forming a new C–C bond.

choices.text: By adding to the carbonyl group of the alkyl halide
choices.why: Alkyl halides have no carbonyl group. The enolate displaces the halide ion.

explanation: Because they're negatively charged, enolate ions act as nucleophiles. They react with primary alkyl halides in the S_N2 reaction, displacing halide ion and forming a new C–C bond, a powerful method for building larger molecules from smaller ones.

prompt: When acetaldehyde, CH3CHO, is treated with base, two molecules combine to give the product known as aldol. How many carbon atoms does aldol contain?
explanation: Two two-carbon acetaldehyde molecules combine, so the product, 3-hydroxybutanal, has 2 + 2 = 4 carbons. Its name, aldol, reflects that it is both an aldehyde and an alcohol.

prompt: A carbonyl condensation reaction is a combination of which two kinds of steps?

choices.text: A nucleophilic addition step and an α-substitution step
Two nucleophilic acyl substitution steps
choices.why: No leaving group is expelled in the acetaldehyde condensation. The steps are α substitution and nucleophilic addition.

choices.text: An electrophilic addition step and an E1 step
choices.why: Those are alkene and alcohol reactions. Carbonyl condensation combines α substitution with nucleophilic addition.

choices.text: A nucleophilic acyl substitution step and an S_N2 step
choices.why: The enolate of one molecule adds to the carbonyl group of another: α substitution plus nucleophilic addition.

explanation: A carbonyl condensation reaction is simply a combination of a nucleophilic addition step and an α-substitution step. The enolate ion of one acetaldehyde molecule acts as a nucleophile and adds to the carbonyl group of another acetaldehyde molecule, giving 3-hydroxybutanal (Figure 18.14.5).

prompt: Cyanide ion, CN−, adds to the carbonyl group of acetone, (CH3)2C=O, and the product is protonated to give an alcohol. What is the product?

choices.text: (CH3)2C(OH)CN
CH3COCN
choices.why: That would require loss of a methyl group as a leaving group, but ketones have no leaving group.

choices.text: NCCH2COCH3
choices.why: Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon; it doesn't replace an α hydrogen.

choices.text: (CH3)2CHOH
choices.why: That is the product of hydride reduction. Here the nucleophile is cyanide.

explanation: Cyanide adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide that is protonated to an alcohol. The former carbonyl carbon ends up bonded to –OH, –CN, and the two methyl groups (Exercise 18.14.2).

prompt: Acetyl chloride reacts with ammonia to give acetamide. Which kind of carbonyl reaction is this?

choices.text: Nucleophilic acyl substitution
Nucleophilic addition
choices.why: A leaving group (chloride) is replaced by the nucleophile, so this is acyl substitution.

choices.text: Alpha substitution
choices.why: The reaction takes place at the carbonyl carbon, not at the α position.

choices.text: Carbonyl condensation
choices.why: Only one carbonyl compound takes part, so this is not a condensation.

explanation: Ammonia adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels chloride ion. Replacing the leaving group with the nucleophile is nucleophilic acyl substitution, like the conversion of acid chlorides into esters by alkoxide ions (Exercise 18.14.3a).

prompt: Acetaldehyde reacts with hydroxylamine to give acetaldoxime. Which kind of carbonyl reaction is this?

choices.text: Nucleophilic addition
Nucleophilic acyl substitution
choices.why: Acetaldehyde is an aldehyde with no leaving group; acyl substitution occurs only with carboxylic acid derivatives.

choices.text: Alpha substitution
choices.why: The nucleophile reacts at the carbonyl carbon, not at the α position.

choices.text: Carbonyl condensation
choices.why: Only one carbonyl compound takes part, so this is not a condensation.

explanation: Hydroxylamine, an amine-type nucleophile, adds to the aldehyde's carbonyl carbon, and the tetrahedral intermediate then loses water to form a C=N bond. This is the C=Nu mode of nucleophilic addition (Exercise 18.14.3b).

prompt: Two molecules of cyclopentanone react with NaOH to give a product in which a cyclopentanol ring is bonded to a cyclopentanone ring. Which kind of carbonyl reaction is this?

choices.text: Carbonyl condensation
Nucleophilic acyl substitution
choices.why: Cyclopentanone is a ketone, which has no leaving group.

choices.text: Nucleophilic addition
choices.why: An addition step does occur, but two carbonyl compounds joining through an enolate is a carbonyl condensation.

choices.text: Alpha substitution
choices.why: An α-substitution step occurs, but combined with addition to a second carbonyl molecule it makes a carbonyl condensation.

explanation: When two carbonyl compounds react with each other in base, the enolate ion of one adds to the carbonyl group of the other. This combination of α substitution and nucleophilic addition is a carbonyl condensation (Exercise 18.14.3c).
